page: Amazon Web Services m2.xlarge is a legacy memory-skewed instance powered by a dual-core Intel Xeon E5-2665 processor operating at 2.4 GHz. Built on the Xen hypervisor with an x86_64 architecture, it provisions two dedicated physical cores without simultaneous multithreading, providing 17.0 GB of system memory (8.55 GB per vCPU) and a 20 MB L3 cache. It incorporates 420 GB of bundled local magnetic HDD storage and lacks dedicated GPU hardware acceleration.

Benchmark evaluations highlight the aging microarchitecture and limited instruction set support. With modern vector extensions such as AVX and AVX-512 unavailable, compute-intensive operations score low, achieving a Geekbench single-core score of 651.0 and a multi-core score of 778.0. Multi-core stress-ng performance reaches 1,719.98, and PassMark CPU overall scores 1,270.65. Uncached large-block read memory bandwidth measures 13.55 GB/sec, while static web serving throughput registers at 1.67 GB/sec, placing this instance within the lower tier of modern cloud compute benchmarks.

The primary tradeoff of the m2.xlarge centers on its legacy profile: substantial memory capacity coupled with modest compute capability and slow mechanical storage. In modern contexts, resource cost efficiency is low compared to newer generations that provide faster per-core compute, hardware encryption, and solid-state storage. It remains suited primarily for legacy enterprise workloads, background batch jobs, and small staging environments that depend on higher RAM allocations without demanding modern instruction sets or high disk IOPS.
description: Amazon Web Services m2.xlarge is a legacy virtual machine provisioned on the Xen hypervisor, equipped with two dedicated Intel Xeon E5-2665 cores running at 2.4 GHz on x86_64 architecture. The server provides 17.0 GB of RAM, equating to an 8.55 GB per-core allocation, along with 420 GB of local HDD storage and no GPU acceleration. Benchmark measurements reflect its legacy status: multi-core Geekbench scores reach 778.0, PassMark CPU reaches 1,270.65, and uncached large-block read memory bandwidth achieves 13.55 GB/sec. Due to the absence of modern vector extensions and reliance on mechanical disk storage, overall throughput and compute performance place in the lower quartile of current cloud standards. The m2.xlarge is primarily suited for maintaining legacy applications, small-scale relational databases, or memory-heavy background tasks that do not require high computational density or modern cryptographic acceleration.
